title: Board appeals where a lobbyist reported contacts about the project
question: When a lobbyist reported contacting officials about a project, did the Board decide that project’s appeal differently?
finding: Of 164 appeals decided by a vote, 64 concern a file or address a lobbyist reported contacting officials about; the Board upheld 23 of them (35.9%) against 17 of the other 100 (17.0%). Holding the kind of appeal fixed, 17.4 would be expected; 1.6% of 5,000 shuffles reach 23. The papers identify the project sponsor in 216 of 251 hearing files.
how: Appeals and their outcomes are those of the votes screens (hearing file and sibling motions, 2015-2026). A contact counts when the lobbyist’s report names the Board file number of the hearing or a sibling motion, or names the same street number and street within two years before to one year after the appeal was filed. Upheld means the Board reversed the decision or approved the project again under its own conditions. Sponsor classifications use explicit identifications in Planning papers, Board attachments or hearing minutes. Where the sponsor and hearing appear in separate documents, the record number or project and parcel must agree. Individuals are counted by category. Mixed private and public sponsors are counted together. A professional named as sponsor is classified separately when the document does not identify the person or organization they represent. Each reviewed file includes the primary document and PDF page.
limits: Lobbyists are hired most for large and contested projects, which also draw the appeals that succeed, so this shows a difference, not a cause. Contacts come from both sides; most sought approval of the project. The address match can catch another project at the same address. Some files lack a record that explicitly identifies the sponsor. The contact and vote comparison uses the same hearing population regardless of whether a sponsor is identified.
